previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A male patient was admitted with pleuritic chest pain and left lower quadrant abdominal pain, both starting two days prior. He had stopped his Lovenox due to running out of the prescription. Workup including CT imaging and cardiac enzymes ruled out pulmonary embolism, acute coronary syndrome, and intra-abdominal pathology. Pain was managed with diclofenac and a PPI, avoiding opioids due to a history of medication abuse. Lovenox was restarted at a lower, once-daily dose for prophylaxis. The patient was discharged home with follow-up arranged with primary care and the chronic pain clinic. His condition at discharge was stable with normal oxygen saturation.

Brief Hospital Course:
Admitted from OSH to the vascular service on ___. It was 
determined that he would be managed medicalled. He was continued 
on a heparin gtt with good blood pressure management. Upon 
admission to the floor he did have some hemoptysis and heparin 
was temporarily held, and restarted in several hours. On HD 2 a 
hematology consult was called due to his history of factor V 
Leiden and multiple pulmonary emboli and deep venous thromboses 
and now with aortic arch thrombus. A pulmonary consult was also 
called given his h/o hemoptysis over the past month.

Heme impression:
While he does have factor V Leiden, this does not typically 
cause arterial thromboseswarranted to rule out antiphospholipid 
antibody syndrome in this patient.  We recommend checking 
anticardiolipin antibodies.  We also recommend checking beta-2 
microglobulin 1 antibody.  He should eventually also have a 
lupus anticoagulant
checked; however, this cannot be done while on heparin.
Other possibilities for arterial thrombosis include paroxysmal
nocturnal hemoglobinuria, polycythemia ___, and essential
thrombocythemia; however, he does not appear to have these
conditions based on review of his CBC. More likely, his arterial 
event is due to the presence of multiple cardiovascular risk 
factors (eg, obesity, hypertension,
smoking, hyperlipidemia, hypertension, and possible diabetes).
These should be controlled in any event.
We recommend continued heparin drip while as an inpatient and
when it is time for discharge, he can be transitioned to his
usual dose of Lovenox, which would be at the 1.5 mg/kg per day
dosing, which he is taking, that is 150 mg subcutaneously once
daily. We recommend that he follow up with our outpatient 
coagulation
clinic.  We also agree with followup imaging to evaluate this
thrombus within the next week.

Pulm impression:
With pristine parenchyma,little concern for DAH or 
infectious/inflammatory process
contributing to hemoptysis.  There is no evidence of large PE, 
and while small peripheral PEs may be present but unidentified 
on CT especially in this gentleman, this would not change 
current management. He had a recent bronchitis, which could be 
enough to cause some mild bleeding in setting of 
anticoagulation.  With
little concern for endobronchial lesion, and again, no evidence 
parenchymal process, there is currently no role/need for 
bronchoscopy.  No contraindication from pulmonary perspective 
for anticoagulation, as Ao thrombus a greater threat currently. 
If hemoptysis worsens, will readdress need for bronchoscopy. 
Continue Advair, albuterol. - PFTs, can be pursued as an 
outpatient.

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  ___ man with reported aortic arch thrombus from outside
hospital.  Please evaluate for aortic arch.

TECHNIQUE:
Initially, non-enhanced CT images of the chest were performed.  Subsequently,
CT angiography of the chest was done after administration of intravenous
contrast.
Coronal, sagittal, and oblique reformats were acquired.

COMPARISON:  CT of the chest from ___.

FINDINGS:
There is an eccentric endophytic thrombus 10 x 28 mm in the proximal
descending aorta distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery.  The
thrombus has a broad-based attachment to the anterior aortic wall.  There is
no evidence of additional thrombi including no evidence of cardiac thrombi. 
There is no evidence of aortic dissection or aortic aneurysm.  The partially
visualized supra-aortic branches are normal.  There is no evidence of
pulmonary embolism.  The lungs are clear.  There is no pleural effusion and no
pericardial effusion.  There is no mediastinal, hilar, or axillary
lymphadenopathy.

The partially visualized liver appears normal.  There are no bony or soft
tissue abnormalities.

IMPRESSION:
1. Large endophytic thrombus in the proximal descending aorta as above.  In
comparison to priors, this formed in an area where much subtler, plaue-like
thrombus was previously noted.  Consider underlying pro-thrombotic conditions
and/or intervening catheter manipulation.  
2. No pulmonary embolism.

Non-invasive venous study of both right and left lower extremities on ___
___. 

All of the deep veins of both right and left lower extremities show normal and
easy compressibility from the groin to below the popliteal bifurcation
bilaterally.  Color flow and pulse Doppler waveforms are normal throughout.

CONCLUSION:  No evidence of DVT in right or left lower extremity.
